metadata.title: Urinary tract infection in under 16s: diagnosis and management
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the diagnosis and management of first or recurrent upper and lower urinary tract infection in babies, children and young people under 16. It covers urine testing, antibiotic treatment, imaging, recurrence prevention, follow-up and information for families. It excludes those with urinary catheters in situ, neurogenic bladders, significant pre-existing urinary tract disorders, underlying renal disease or immunosuppression, as well as those in intensive care and sexually active girls and young women under 16 with recurrent UTI.

target_population: Babies, children and young people from birth up to the age of 16 years with first or recurrent UTI

therapies_index.name: antibiotics
approved_indications: Suspected UTI in babies and children between 3 months and 3 years when leukocyte esterase or nitrite, or both, are positive.
UTI in children aged 3 years or older when both leukocyte esterase and nitrite are positive.
Acute upper UTI in babies and children over 3 months.
Lower UTI in babies and children over 3 months.

therapies_index.name: parenteral antibiotics
approved_indications: Suspected UTI in babies under 3 months under the care of a paediatric specialist.
therapies_index.administration: Parenteral; the guideline does not specify a regimen.

therapies_index.name: prophylactic antibiotics
approved_indications: Prophylaxis when a baby or child undergoes MCUG. For recurrent UTI, the guideline refers to separate NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidance.
therapies_index.administration: Give orally for 3 days when MCUG is performed, scheduling MCUG on the second day.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Manage dysfunctional elimination syndromes and constipation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Babies and children who have had a UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Encourage sufficient water intake to prevent dehydration.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children who have had a UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Provide access to clean toilets when needed so that voiding is not unnecessarily postponed.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children who have had a UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not routinely prescribe prophylactic antibiotics after a first-time UTI.
prophylaxis.target_population: Babies and children following first-time UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consult the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (recurrent): antimicrobial prescribing for prophylactic antibiotic treatment.
prophylaxis.target_population: Babies and children with recurrent UTI
Babies and children with asymptomatic bacteriuria

prophylaxis.recommendation: When MCUG is performed, give oral prophylactic antibiotics, scheduling MCUG for the second day.

infection_management.prevention: After a UTI, address dysfunctional elimination syndromes and constipation, encourage enough water to avoid dehydration, and ensure access to clean toilets without unnecessary delay in voiding.
infection_management.management: Collect a urine sample before giving antibiotics to children and young people. In babies and children at high risk of serious illness, obtain a sample but do not delay treatment if collection is unsuccessful. Refer those at high risk of serious illness immediately to a paediatric specialist. Laboratories should monitor resistance patterns among urinary pathogens and routinely provide that information to prescribers.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Suspected UTI in babies under 3 months
infection_management.management: Refer immediately for paediatric specialist care and send urine for urgent microscopy and culture. Paediatric specialists should administer parenteral antibiotics in accordance with the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management.
For babies and children over 3 months, consider referral to a paediatric specialist and give antibiotics in accordance with the NICE guideline on pyelonephritis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing.
For babies and children over 3 months, give antibiotics in accordance with the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing.

infection_management.prevention: For prophylactic antibiotic treatment in babies and children, consult the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (recurrent): antimicrobial prescribing.
infection_management.management: Refer babies and children with recurrent UTI for assessment by a paediatric specialist. For a UTI arising while a baby or child is already taking prophylactic antibiotics, consult the NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidelines on pyelonephritis (acute), urinary tract infection (lower) and urinary tract infection (recurrent).

infection_management.prevention: Do not prescribe prophylactic antibiotics to babies and children with asymptomatic bacteriuria.
infection_management.management: Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in babies and children with antibiotics, or arrange follow-up solely because it is present.
Assess and manage in accordance with the NICE guideline on sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Suspected or confirmed bacterial infection in babies of up to and including 28 days corrected gestational age
infection_management.management: Assess and manage in accordance with the NICE guideline on neonatal infection: antibiotics for prevention and treatment.

conditions.name: urinary tract infection (UTI)
conditions.description: A bacterial infection of the urinary tract in babies, children and young people under 16. Its diagnosis can be difficult, particularly in children younger than 3 years, because symptoms may be nonspecific and urine collection and interpretation can be challenging.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline describes UTI as a common bacterial infection in babies and children but provides no incidence figure.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Features that increase the likelihood of UTI include dysuria, increased urinary frequency, new bedwetting, malodorous, dark or cloudy urine, visible haematuria, reduced fluid intake, fever, shivering, abdominal pain, loin or suprapubic tenderness, capillary refill longer than 3 seconds, and a history of confirmed UTI. Absence of dysuria, nappy rash, breathing difficulties, abnormal chest or ear findings, and fever with a known alternative cause decrease its likelihood but do not necessarily exclude it. The list is not exhaustive; isolated findings should be interpreted with clinical judgement, and multiple findings probably increase the likelihood of UTI.

subtypes.name: acute upper UTI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In babies and children, bacteriuria with fever of 38°C or higher, or bacteriuria with fever lower than 38°C plus loin pain or tenderness, supports this diagnosis.

subtypes.name: lower UTI (cystitis)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Bacteriuria without systemic symptoms or signs supports this diagnosis in babies and children.

subtypes.name: atypical UTI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Features include serious illness, poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or infection with non-E. coli organisms.

subtypes.name: recurrent UTI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Defined by Two or more episodes of UTI with acute upper UTI; One episode of UTI with acute upper UTI plus 1 or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI; or Three or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Obtain a specimen for testing before antibiotics are given to children and young people.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Test when symptoms or signs increase the likelihood of UTI; consider testing an unwell patient if UTI remains suspected despite the absence of listed features. Do not routinely test those aged 3 months and over whose findings suggest another infection, but consider testing if they remain unwell and the diagnosis is uncertain. Collect without delay, ideally obtaining a sample returned within 24 hours if collection at the consultation is not possible.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Clean catch is preferred where possible. If it is not feasible, use another non-invasive method such as a urine collection pad; if non-invasive collection is impractical or impossible, use a catheter specimen or suprapubic aspiration (SPA). Confirm urine in the bladder by ultrasound before SPA. Do not use cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels for collection.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urine dipstick testing for leukocyte esterase and nitrite
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Guide the diagnosis, need for culture and antibiotic decisions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use in babies and children between 3 months and 3 years with suspected UTI, and follow the age-specific strategy for children 3 years or older.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Between 3 months and 3 years, either positive result calls for culture and antibiotics; when both are negative, do not give antibiotics or send microscopy and culture unless a culture criterion applies. At 3 years or older, two positive results support treating UTI, with culture for high or intermediate risk of serious illness or previous UTI. Positive nitrite with negative leukocyte esterase calls for culture and, if the specimen is fresh, antibiotics. Positive leukocyte esterase with negative nitrite calls for microscopy and culture; give antibiotics only if there is good clinical evidence of UTI. Two negative results support seeking another cause rather than treating or culturing for UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess pyuria and bacteriuria.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain urgently, with culture, for suspected UTI in babies under 3 months; obtain with culture for children 3 years or older whose dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and negative for nitrite.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Bacteriuria supports UTI whether or not pyuria is present. Pyuria without bacteriuria supports starting antibiotics if UTI symptoms or signs are present. If both are absent, assume UTI is absent. Clinical findings should guide decisions when a negative urine result conflicts with the presentation because false negatives can occur.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected UTI and inform subsequent management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Send for suspected acute upper UTI, high to intermediate risk of serious illness, age under 3 months, positive leukocyte esterase or nitrite, recurrent UTI, symptoms and signs inconsistent with dipstick findings, or failure to respond within 24 to 48 hours when no specimen has yet been sent. Additional indications depend on the age-specific dipstick strategy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If culture cannot occur within 4 hours of collection, refrigerate the specimen immediately or preserve it with boric acid, following the manufacturer's instructions for specimen volume.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify factors associated with UTI or serious underlying pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After UTI is confirmed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Record poor urine flow, suspected or confirmed previous UTI, recurrent unexplained fever, an antenatally identified renal abnormality, family history of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) or renal disease, constipation, dysfunctional voiding, enlarged bladder, abdominal mass, signs of a spinal lesion, poor growth and high blood pressure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect structural abnormalities, including obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During an atypical acute infection and otherwise according to age, response to treatment and recurrence. In toilet-trained children, perform it with a full bladder and estimate bladder volume before and after urination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect renal parenchymal defects.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Perform 4 to 6 months after the acute infection when indicated by the age-specific imaging schedules. If another UTI occurs while awaiting the scan, review its timing and consider an earlier scan.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate VUR in selected circumstances rather than routinely.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use according to the age-specific imaging schedules. Between 6 months and under 3 years, consider it if ultrasound shows dilatation, urine flow is poor, infection involves non-E. coli, or there is a family history of VUR.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm or exclude acute upper UTI when localisation is clinically important.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use only in rare instances when confirmation or exclusion matters clinically.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assessment of UTI localisation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Do not use this test alone to distinguish acute upper UTI from lower UTI in babies and children.

follow_up.schedule: Do not routinely arrange follow-up for babies and children who have not undergone imaging, or outpatient follow-up when investigation results are normal. Do not routinely retest urine when the patient is asymptomatic after UTI.
recommended_tests: For renal parenchymal defects, assess height, weight, blood pressure and proteinuria.
Arrange paediatric specialist assessment for recurrent UTI or abnormal imaging.
Arrange monitoring by a paediatric nephrologist for bilateral renal abnormalities, impaired kidney function, raised blood pressure or proteinuria.
long_term_effects: UTI and VUR in young children are associated with congenital and acquired renal damage.
Progressive renal scarring is documented in children with high grade VUR and recurrent UTI.

Renal scarring has been associated with severe hypertension, proteinuria, complications in pregnancy and established renal failure; the frequency and magnitude of these risks in unilateral and bilateral renal damage remain unclear.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Do not offer long-term follow-up solely for minor, unilateral renal parenchymal defects unless recurrent UTI, family history or lifestyle risk factors for hypertension are present. Agree how imaging results will be communicated and provide parents or carers with written results of all investigations.

conditions.name: acute upper UTI
conditions.description: An upper urinary tract infection distinguished clinically from lower UTI by fever and, in some cases, loin pain or tenderness in the presence of bacteriuria.
conditions.clinical_presentation: In babies and children, bacteriuria with fever of 38°C or higher supports acute upper UTI. Bacteriuria with fever lower than 38°C also supports it when accompanied by loin pain or tenderness.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected acute upper UTI.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Send a specimen when acute upper UTI is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assessment of UTI localisation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It should not be used on its own to distinguish acute upper UTI from lower UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm or exclude acute upper UTI.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use in the rare situations where establishing the location is clinically important.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm or exclude acute upper UTI when necessary; after infection, detect renal parenchymal defects when the imaging schedule indicates.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For localisation, use if power doppler ultrasound is unavailable or has not confirmed the diagnosis. For parenchymal assessment, the scheduled timing is 4 to 6 months after acute infection where indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for structural abnormalities when imaging is indicated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Determine timing from age and whether the infection is atypical or recurrent.

follow_up.schedule: Where indicated by the age-specific imaging schedule, perform a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after acute infection; review the timing and consider an earlier scan if another UTI develops while waiting.
recommended_tests: Age- and presentation-specific urinary tract ultrasound.
Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scintigraphy scan when indicated.
long_term_effects: Renal parenchymal defects or scarring may be relevant after UTI.

conditions.name: lower UTI (cystitis)
conditions.description: A lower urinary tract infection diagnosed in babies and children with bacteriuria but no systemic symptoms or signs.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Bacteriuria occurs without systemic symptoms or signs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support the distinction between lower UTI and acute upper UTI.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When UTI is suspected in a baby or child.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Bacteriuria without systemic findings supports lower UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate the urinary tract when imaging criteria are met.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After lower UTI, arrange ultrasound within 6 weeks only for babies younger than 6 months or for those with recurrent infections.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assessment of UTI localisation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Do not use it alone to distinguish lower UTI from acute upper UTI.

follow_up.schedule: After lower UTI, ultrasound within 6 weeks is indicated only when the baby is younger than 6 months or infections are recurrent.
recommended_tests: Urinary tract ultrasound when the age or recurrence criterion is met.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Do not routinely arrange outpatient follow-up if investigation results are normal.

conditions.name: atypical UTI
conditions.description: A UTI meeting any of the guideline's specified features of atypical infection.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Features are serious illness, poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, lack of response to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or infection with non-E. coli organisms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify structural abnormalities such as obstruction so that they can be managed promptly.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Perform during the acute infection for atypical UTI. If non-E. coli UTI responds well to antibiotics and no other atypical feature is present, a non-urgent ultrasound can instead be requested within 6 weeks.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect renal parenchymal defects.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For atypical UTI in babies younger than 6 months and in babies and children from 6 months to under 3 years, the imaging schedules indicate a scan 4 to 6 months after acute infection. The schedule does not indicate this scan for atypical UTI in children 3 years or older.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate VUR in selected patients.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The schedule indicates MCUG for atypical UTI in babies younger than 6 months. It is not scheduled routinely at older ages; from 6 months to under 3 years, consider it if ultrasound shows dilatation, urine flow is poor, infection involves non-E. coli, or there is a family history of VUR.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify raised creatinine as a feature of atypical UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Raised creatinine is among the defining features of atypical UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate infection, including an infection that does not respond to treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Send if treatment has not worked within 24 to 48 hours and no specimen has already been sent.

follow_up.schedule: The imaging schedule varies by age: ultrasound during acute infection at all listed ages; DMSA at 4 to 6 months after acute infection for patients younger than 3 years; and MCUG for babies younger than 6 months. A responding non-E. coli infection without another atypical feature may instead have non-urgent ultrasound within 6 weeks.
recommended_tests: Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scintigraphy scan when age criteria apply.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Abnormal imaging results warrant assessment by a paediatric specialist.

conditions.name: recurrent UTI
conditions.description: Repeated UTI episodes meeting the guideline's combinations of acute upper and lower infections.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The guideline does not establish whether symptoms and signs differ from those in patients without recurrent UTI; it identifies this as a research question.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate recurrent infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Send a specimen when a baby or child has recurrent UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the urinary tract after recurrent infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During acute infection for babies younger than 6 months; within 6 weeks for babies and children from 6 months to under 3 years and for children 3 years or older.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect renal parenchymal defects.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For recurrent UTI across the listed age groups, the imaging schedules indicate scanning 4 to 6 months after acute infection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate VUR in selected circumstances.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The imaging schedule indicates it for recurrent UTI in babies younger than 6 months. It is not scheduled routinely for older children; from 6 months to under 3 years, consider it if ultrasound shows dilatation, urine flow is poor, infection involves non-E. coli, or there is a family history of VUR.

staging.additional_rules: Recurrent UTI means Two or more episodes of UTI with acute upper UTI (acute pyelonephritis), or One episode of UTI with acute upper UTI plus 1 or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI (cystitis), or Three or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI.

follow_up.schedule: Arrange assessment by a paediatric specialist. Imaging timing depends on age: ultrasound during acute infection when younger than 6 months, or within 6 weeks when 6 months or older; DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after acute infection at the ages covered by the schedules.
recommended_tests: Height, weight, blood pressure and proteinuria assessment if renal parenchymal defects are present.
long_term_effects: Progressive renal scarring is documented in children who have both high grade VUR and recurrent UTI.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Recurrent UTI is an exception to the advice against long-term follow-up for minor, unilateral renal parenchymal defects.

conditions.name: first-time UTI
conditions.description: A first UTI episode, for which imaging decisions depend on age, response to treatment and the presence of atypical features.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the urinary tract after a first infection when indicated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For babies younger than 6 months whose infection responds to treatment, perform within 6 weeks. Do not routinely perform it for babies and children over 6 months whose first UTI responds to treatment, unless atypical features are present.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For babies younger than 6 months, consider micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) if this ultrasound is abnormal.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect renal parenchymal defects when indicated by the imaging schedule.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The schedules do not indicate it for an otherwise responsive first-time UTI; atypical features alter the imaging schedule.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate VUR in selected circumstances.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Do not use routinely following a responsive first-time UTI. For a baby younger than 6 months, consider it if the scheduled ultrasound is abnormal.

follow_up.schedule: Following a responsive first-time UTI, perform ultrasound within 6 weeks if the baby is younger than 6 months; do not routinely perform ultrasound in those over 6 months unless the UTI is atypical.
recommended_tests: Urinary tract ultrasound when the age or atypical-infection criterion applies.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Do not routinely provide prophylactic antibiotics after first-time UTI.

conditions.name: asymptomatic bacteriuria
conditions.description: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms; the guideline distinguishes bacteriuria from UTI because bacteria can be present with or without UTI.

follow_up.schedule: Do not follow up babies and children solely because asymptomatic bacteriuria is present.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline advises against antibiotics to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria and against prophylactic antibiotics for this finding.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies under 3 months with suspected UTI
decision_rules: Refer immediately for paediatric specialist care.
Send urine for urgent microscopy and culture.
A paediatric specialist should treat in accordance with the referenced NICE guideline on fever in under 5s.

recommended_regimens.name: parenteral antibiotics
recommended_regimens.summary: A paediatric specialist should administer these for suspected UTI in babies under 3 months, following the referenced NICE guidance.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline does not specify an antibiotic or dose for this population.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies and children at high risk of serious illness
decision_rules: Refer immediately to a paediatric specialist.
Obtain a urine sample, but do not postpone treatment if collection is unsuccessful.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies and children between 3 months and 3 years with suspected UTI
decision_rules: Use a urine dipstick to assess leukocyte esterase and nitrite.
If either result is positive, send urine for culture and give antibiotics.
If both results are negative, do not give antibiotics; send urine for microscopy and culture only if at least 1 criterion in recommendation 1.1.21 applies.

recommended_regimens.name: antibiotics
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat when leukocyte esterase or nitrite, or both, are positive on dipstick testing.

not_recommended.name: antibiotics
not_recommended.reason: Do not give them for suspected UTI when both leukocyte esterase and nitrite are negative.

response_assessment.interpretation: If infection has not responded and no urine sample has already been sent, send one for culture.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline directs antibiotic selection for acute upper or lower UTI to separate NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidelines.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children 3 years or older with suspected UTI
decision_rules: If leukocyte esterase and nitrite are both positive, presume UTI and give antibiotics; also send urine for culture if serious-illness risk is high or intermediate or there is a history of previous UTI.

If leukocyte esterase is negative and nitrite is positive, give antibiotics only when the dipstick was performed on a fresh urine sample. Send urine for culture and use its result to guide subsequent management.

If leukocyte esterase is positive and nitrite is negative, send urine for microscopy and culture. Give antibiotics only if clinical evidence of UTI is strong, such as clear urinary symptoms; consider that the result could indicate infection elsewhere.
If leukocyte esterase and nitrite are both negative, presume UTI is absent, withhold antibiotics for UTI and do not send urine for culture; investigate other possible causes.
Use clinical findings to guide decisions when a urine result conflicts with them, because a false-negative result is possible.

recommended_regimens.name: antibiotics
recommended_regimens.summary: Give for both dipstick markers positive, or for nitrite positive with leukocyte esterase negative when a fresh urine sample was tested.

not_recommended.name: antibiotics
not_recommended.reason: Do not give for a UTI when both dipstick markers are negative; when only leukocyte esterase is positive, withhold them unless clinical evidence of UTI is strong.

response_assessment.method: Review the culture result when nitrite is positive and leukocyte esterase is negative.
response_assessment.interpretation: Base further management on the culture result.
If infection has not responded and no urine sample has already been sent, send one for culture.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Serious-illness risk affects urine testing and interpretation.

decision_rules: Consider referral to a paediatric specialist.
Treat according to the referenced NICE guideline on pyelonephritis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing.
In babies or children, presume acute upper UTI when bacteriuria accompanies fever of 38°C or higher, or when bacteriuria and fever lower than 38°C accompany loin pain or tenderness.

recommended_regimens.name: antibiotics
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat acute upper UTI following the referenced NICE antimicrobial prescribing guideline.

response_assessment.interpretation: Failure to respond is a feature of atypical UTI.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not provide a specific antibiotic regimen or dose.

decision_rules: Treat according to the referenced NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing.
In babies and children, bacteriuria without systemic symptoms or signs supports the lower UTI pathway.

recommended_regimens.name: antibiotics
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat lower UTI following the referenced NICE antimicrobial prescribing guideline.

response_assessment.interpretation: Failure to respond is a feature of atypical UTI.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not provide a specific antibiotic regimen or dose.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies and children with bacteriuria but no symptoms
decision_rules: Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with antibiotics.
Do not give prophylactic antibiotics or arrange follow-up solely because asymptomatic bacteriuria is present.

not_recommended.name: antibiotics
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in babies and children.

not_recommended.name: prophylactic antibiotics
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against prophylaxis for babies and children with asymptomatic bacteriuria.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies and children with recurrent UTI
decision_rules: Refer for assessment by a paediatric specialist.
For prophylactic antibiotic treatment, consult the referenced NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (recurrent): antimicrobial prescribing.
supportive_care: Manage dysfunctional elimination syndromes and constipation after UTI.
Encourage sufficient water intake to avoid dehydration and access to clean toilets without unnecessary delay in voiding.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Recurrent UTI means Two or more episodes of UTI with acute upper UTI (acute pyelonephritis), One episode of UTI with acute upper UTI plus 1 or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI (cystitis), or Three or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI. The document does not specify a prophylactic antibiotic regimen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies and children after first-time UTI
decision_rules: Do not routinely prescribe prophylactic antibiotics following the first UTI.
Manage dysfunctional elimination syndromes and constipation where present.

not_recommended.name: prophylactic antibiotics
not_recommended.reason: Routine prophylaxis after first-time UTI is not recommended.

supportive_care: Encourage children to drink enough water to avoid dehydration.
Ensure children can use clean toilets when needed without unnecessary postponement of voiding.
Advise families that UTI can recur and that suspected reinfection warrants prompt treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies and children for whom confirming or excluding acute upper UTI is clinically important
decision_rules: Do not routinely use imaging to determine the site of UTI.

In the rare situation where confirmation or exclusion of acute upper UTI matters clinically, use power doppler ultrasound; use a dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scintigraphy scan if power doppler ultrasound is unavailable or has not confirmed the diagnosis.

recommended_regimens.name: power doppler ultrasound
recommended_regimens.summary: An imaging option for localising UTI in the rare circumstances specified.

alternative_regimens.name: dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scintigraphy scan
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative imaging option when localisation is clinically important.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use if power doppler ultrasound is unavailable or the diagnosis remains unconfirmed.

not_recommended.name: imaging to localise UTI
not_recommended.reason: Routine use is not recommended; the guideline reserves localisation imaging for rare instances of clinical importance.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Do not rely on C-reactive protein alone to distinguish acute upper from lower UTI.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies younger than 6 months after UTI
decision_rules: For a first-time UTI responding well within 48 hours, arrange ultrasound within 6 weeks; consider micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) if the ultrasound is abnormal. Do not schedule an acute-infection ultrasound, a later dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy scan or MCUG routinely for this response category.
For atypical UTI or recurrent UTI, perform ultrasound during the acute infection, a dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy scan 4 to 6 months after the acute infection, and MCUG.
If a non-E. coli UTI responds well to antibiotics without other atypical features, a non-urgent ultrasound within 6 weeks can be requested.
If another UTI occurs while a DMSA scan is pending, review its timing and consider performing it sooner.

recommended_regimens.name: ultrasound
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform within 6 weeks for first-time UTI responding to treatment, or during the acute infection for atypical or recurrent UTI.

recommended_regimens.name: dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Assess for renal parenchymal defects after atypical or recurrent UTI.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 4 to 6 months after the acute infection

recommended_regimens.name: micturating cystourethrogram
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform after atypical or recurrent UTI; consider it after an abnormal ultrasound in the responding first-time UTI category.

response_assessment.interpretation: The imaging schedule differs according to response and whether UTI is atypical or recurrent.

supportive_care: When MCUG is performed, give prophylactic antibiotics orally for 3 days, scheduling MCUG on the second day.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Atypical UTI includes serious illness, poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or infection with non-E. coli organisms.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Babies and children between 6 months to under 3 years after UTI
decision_rules: If UTI responds well to treatment within 48 hours, do not routinely perform the imaging tests listed for this age group.
For atypical UTI, perform ultrasound during the acute infection and a dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy scan 4 to 6 months later.
For recurrent UTI, perform ultrasound within 6 weeks and a dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy scan 4 to 6 months after the acute infection.
Do not perform MCUG routinely; consider it if ultrasound shows dilatation, urine flow is poor, infection is non-E. coli, or there is a family history of VUR.
If a non-E. coli UTI responds well to antibiotics and has no other atypical features, a non-urgent ultrasound within 6 weeks can be requested.
If another UTI occurs while a DMSA scan is pending, review its timing and consider performing it sooner.

recommended_regimens.name: ultrasound
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform during atypical infection or within 6 weeks for recurrent UTI, subject to the stated exception for an otherwise well-responding non-E. coli infection.

recommended_regimens.name: dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Assess for renal parenchymal defects after atypical or recurrent UTI.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 4 to 6 months after the acute infection

special_populations.considerations: Use a urine dipstick. If both leukocyte esterase and nitrite are negative, do not routinely send urine for microscopy and culture unless a criterion in recommendation 1.1.21 applies. If either or both are positive, send the sample for culture.

special_populations.population: Babies and children younger than 6 months after UTI
special_populations.considerations: After a first UTI that responds to treatment, arrange ultrasound within 6 weeks. During atypical or recurrent infection, arrange ultrasound in the acute phase, followed by a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after the infection and a micturating cystourethrogram.

special_populations.population: Babies and children between 6 months to under 3 years after UTI
special_populations.considerations: The imaging schedule distinguishes a good response within 48 hours, atypical infection and recurrent infection. Atypical infection calls for ultrasound during the acute illness; recurrent infection calls for ultrasound within 6 weeks. Both call for a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after the acute infection. Micturating cystourethrogram is not routine, but should be considered if there is ultrasound dilatation, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection or a family history of VUR.

special_populations.population: Children 3 years or older after UTI
special_populations.considerations: Atypical infection calls for ultrasound during the acute illness. Recurrent infection calls for ultrasound within 6 weeks and a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after the acute infection. Routine micturating cystourethrogram is not indicated.

special_populations.population: Babies and children with non-E. coli urinary tract infection responding well to antibiotics and no other atypical features

special_populations.population: Babies and children with recurrent UTI or abnormal imaging results

special_populations.population: Babies and children with asymptomatic bacteriuria

special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use antibiotics to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria or give prophylactic antibiotics for it.

special_populations.population: Babies and children with renal parenchymal defects
special_populations.considerations: Assessment should include height, weight, blood pressure and routine testing for proteinuria. Do not offer long-term follow-up for minor, unilateral defects unless recurrent UTI, family history or lifestyle risk factors for hypertension are present.

special_populations.population: Babies and children with bilateral renal abnormalities, impaired kidney function, raised blood pressure or proteinuria

special_populations.population: Babies and children who have had a UTI and have dysfunctional elimination syndromes or constipation
special_populations.considerations: Manage the dysfunctional elimination syndrome or constipation as part of preventing recurrence.

special_populations.population: Babies and children with conditions outside the guideline's scope

special_populations.treatment_modifications: Antibiotic requirements for conditions outside its scope, including significant pre-existing uropathies, are not addressed and may differ from those described in the guideline.

recommendations.statement: Test urine in babies, children and young people who have symptoms or signs that increase the likelihood of a urinary tract infection (UTI).
recommendations.context: Use table 1 and its accompanying guidance to inform the decision; no single symptom or sign should necessarily determine whether testing is needed.
recommendations.rationale: Prompt, accurate diagnosis may prevent unnecessary suffering and complications such as renal scarring. The symptom and sign evidence was often of low or very low quality, so clinical judgement remains important.

recommendations.statement: Consider a urine test for an unwell baby, child or young person when UTI is suspected, even if none of the symptoms or signs in table 1 is present.
recommendations.rationale: The list in table 1 is not exhaustive, and its absence should not prevent further investigation of a possible UTI.

recommendations.statement: Refer babies under 3 months with suspected UTI for paediatric specialist care. Send urine for urgent microscopy and culture, and manage them according to the sections on non-paediatric and paediatric specialist management in the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management.
recommendations.rationale: The committee identified concern about sepsis in this age group and favoured specialist referral over management of symptoms by the GP.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely test urine in babies, children or young people aged 3 months or over whose symptoms and signs suggest an infection other than UTI. Consider testing if they remain unwell and the diagnosis is uncertain.
recommendations.rationale: Routine testing in this situation may be clinically unnecessary, use resources and cause distress; persistent illness with diagnostic uncertainty may warrant testing to exclude UTI.

recommendations.statement: For babies or children under 5 with fever without an evident cause when UTI is no longer suspected, consult the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management.
recommendations.rationale: That guideline provides guidance on identifying the cause of fever.

recommendations.statement: Paediatric specialists caring for babies and children under 5 with fever should consult the paediatric specialist management section of the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management for guidance on when to test urine for UTI.

Collect and test urine without delay. If collection cannot take place during the consultation, advise parents or carers, as appropriate, to collect and return the sample as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.
recommendations.rationale: The committee sought to support rapid, accurate diagnosis despite practical delays in obtaining samples.

recommendations.statement: Assess and manage a baby, child or young person with suspected sepsis according to the NICE guideline on sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management.

For a baby of up to and including 28 days corrected gestational age with suspected or confirmed bacterial infection, follow the NICE guideline on neonatal infection: antibiotics for prevention and treatment, using its relevant sections for early-onset or late-onset neonatal infection.
Assess illness severity in babies and children using the clinical assessment section of the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management.

recommendations.statement: Obtain urine samples from children and young people before administering antibiotics.
recommendations.context: The recommendation is aligned with the NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidelines on pyelonephritis (acute) and urinary tract infection (lower).

recommendations.statement: Obtain a urine sample from babies and children at high risk of serious illness, but do not delay treatment if a sample cannot be obtained.
Use clean catch to collect urine whenever possible.
If clean catch is not feasible, use another non-invasive collection method, such as a urine collection pad, following the manufacturer's instructions for pads.
Do not collect urine from babies or children using cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels.
Use catheter sampling or suprapubic aspiration (SPA) if non-invasive urine collection is impossible or impractical. Before SPA, use ultrasound guidance to verify that the bladder contains urine.
Immediately refrigerate a urine specimen intended for culture, or preserve it with boric acid, if culture cannot be performed within 4 hours of collection.
When preserving urine with boric acid, follow the manufacturer's instructions on specimen volume to avoid possible toxicity to bacteria in the sample.

Use a urine dipstick in babies and children between 3 months and 3 years with suspected UTI. If leukocyte esterase and nitrite are both negative, do not give antibiotics and do not request microscopy and culture unless at least 1 criterion in recommendation 1.1.21 applies. If leukocyte esterase or nitrite, or both, are positive, send urine for culture and give antibiotics.
recommendations.rationale: A positive result for either marker greatly increases the likelihood of a positive culture; culturing positive samples offers a better balance of benefits and costs than culturing and treating all children in this age group.

recommendations.statement: For children aged 3 years or older, follow the table 2 urine dipstick strategy. When leukocyte esterase and nitrite are both positive, presume UTI and give antibiotics; send urine for culture if serious-illness risk is high or intermediate or there is a previous UTI. When leukocyte esterase is negative and nitrite positive, give antibiotics if the tested urine was fresh, send it for culture and base subsequent management on the culture result. When leukocyte esterase is positive and nitrite negative, send urine for microscopy and culture, but withhold antibiotics unless there is good clinical evidence of UTI. When both are negative, presume UTI is absent, do not prescribe antibiotics for UTI or send a culture, and investigate other possible causes.
recommendations.context: Assess serious-illness risk using the clinical assessment section of the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management; age and illness risk affect the choice and interpretation of urine tests.

recommendations.statement: Send a baby or child's urine for culture when acute upper UTI is suspected; serious-illness risk is high or intermediate; the baby is under 3 months; leukocyte esterase or nitrite is positive; UTI is recurrent; infection has not responded within 24 to 48 hours and no sample has yet been sent; or symptoms and signs conflict with dipstick results.

Interpret urine microscopy according to table 3: presume UTI if both pyuria and bacteriuria are present or if bacteriuria is present without pyuria; if pyuria is present without bacteriuria, start antibiotics when UTI symptoms or signs are present; if both findings are absent, presume there is no UTI.
Base decisions on clinical criteria when urine test results do not support the clinical findings.
recommendations.rationale: A small number of discordant tests may be false negatives.

recommendations.statement: Document risk factors for UTI and serious underlying pathology: poor urine flow; suspected or confirmed previous UTI; recurrent fever without a clear cause; an antenatally identified renal abnormality; family history of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) or renal disease; constipation; dysfunctional voiding; enlarged bladder; abdominal mass; signs of a spinal lesion; poor growth; and high blood pressure.

recommendations.statement: Presume acute upper UTI in a baby or child with bacteriuria and fever of 38°C or higher, or with bacteriuria, fever lower than 38°C and loin pain or tenderness.

recommendations.statement: Presume lower UTI (cystitis) in babies and children with bacteriuria but no systemic symptoms or signs.

recommendations.statement: Do not rely on C-reactive protein alone to distinguish acute upper UTI from lower UTI in babies or children.

recommendations.statement: Immediately refer babies and children at high risk of serious illness to a paediatric specialist.
Immediately refer a baby under 3 months with suspected UTI to a paediatric specialist.

Paediatric specialists should give parenteral antibiotics to babies under 3 months with suspected UTI, following the paediatric specialist management section of the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s.
Consider referral to a paediatric specialist for babies and children over 3 months with upper UTI.
Treat acute upper UTI in babies and children over 3 months with antibiotics according to the NICE guideline on pyelonephritis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing.
Treat lower UTI in babies and children over 3 months with antibiotics according to the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing.

For treatment of UTI arising while a baby or child is already receiving prophylactic antibiotics, consult the NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidelines on pyelonephritis (acute), urinary tract infection (lower) and urinary tract infection (recurrent).
Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in babies or children with antibiotics.
Laboratories should track urinary pathogen resistance patterns and routinely provide that information to prescribers.
Manage dysfunctional elimination syndromes and constipation in babies and children who have experienced a UTI.
Encourage children with a previous UTI to drink sufficient water to prevent dehydration.
Ensure children who have had a UTI can use clean toilets when needed without unnecessary postponement of urination.
Do not routinely prescribe prophylactic antibiotics to babies or children after their first UTI.
For prophylactic antibiotic treatment of recurrent UTI in babies and children, consult the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (recurrent): antimicrobial prescribing.
Do not give prophylactic antibiotics to babies or children with asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Do not routinely use imaging to establish the location of a UTI.

recommendations.statement: In rare circumstances when confirmation or exclusion of acute upper UTI is clinically important, use power doppler ultrasound; use a dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scintigraphy scan if power doppler ultrasound is unavailable or has not confirmed the diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Arrange urinary tract ultrasound during the acute infection for babies and children with atypical UTI, following tables 4, 5 and 6.
recommendations.context: The guideline defines atypical UTI as including serious illness, poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or infection with non-E. coli organisms.
recommendations.rationale: The scan is intended to identify structural abnormalities, including obstruction, so that management can occur promptly.

recommendations.statement: Arrange ultrasound within 6 weeks of the UTI for babies younger than 6 months whose first UTI responds to treatment, as specified in table 4.
Do not routinely arrange ultrasound for babies and children over 6 months whose first UTI responds to treatment, unless the UTI is atypical, as set out in tables 5 and 6.
After a lower UTI, arrange ultrasound within 6 weeks only for babies and children younger than 6 months or those with recurrent infections.
Use a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after the acute infection to identify renal parenchymal defects in babies and children when indicated by tables 4, 5 and 6.
If a baby or child develops another UTI while awaiting a DMSA scan, reassess its timing and consider performing it earlier.
Do not routinely image babies and children after UTI to detect VUR, apart from the specified circumstances in tables 4, 5 and 6.
When performing a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG), give oral prophylactic antibiotics for 3 days and perform the MCUG on the second day.
Arrange imaging after UTI in babies and children according to the age- and presentation-specific schedules in tables 4, 5 and 6.
recommendations.context: For babies younger than 6 months, table 4 specifies ultrasound during acute atypical or recurrent UTI, ultrasound within 6 weeks after a treatment-responsive UTI, and a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after atypical or recurrent UTI; it also specifies MCUG for atypical or recurrent UTI. For those between 6 months to under 3 years, table 5 specifies acute ultrasound for atypical UTI, ultrasound within 6 weeks for recurrent UTI, and a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after atypical or recurrent UTI; MCUG is not routine but should be considered with ultrasound dilatation, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection or family history of VUR. For children 3 years or older, table 6 specifies acute ultrasound for atypical UTI and ultrasound within 6 weeks plus a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after recurrent UTI. The tables also provide qualifications for a treatment-responsive non-E. coli UTI without other atypical features and for ultrasound in toilet-trained children.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely use surgery to manage VUR.
Do not routinely provide follow-up for babies and children who have not undergone imaging investigations.
Agree with parents, carers or the young person, as appropriate, how imaging results will be communicated.
Do not routinely offer outpatient follow-up appointments when investigation results are normal.
Provide parents or carers with written results of every investigation.
Refer babies and children with recurrent UTI or abnormal imaging findings for assessment by a paediatric specialist.
Include height, weight, blood pressure and routine proteinuria testing when assessing babies and children with renal parenchymal defects.
Do not offer long-term follow-up for babies and children with minor, unilateral renal parenchymal defects unless they have recurrent UTI, a family history or lifestyle risk factors for hypertension.
Arrange monitoring and appropriate management by a paediatric nephrologist for babies and children with bilateral renal abnormalities, impaired kidney function, raised blood pressure or proteinuria.
recommendations.rationale: The stated aim is to slow progression of chronic kidney disease.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely repeat urine testing for infection after a UTI episode in babies and children who have no symptoms.
Do not follow up babies or children solely because asymptomatic bacteriuria is present.

When UTI is suspected in a child or young person, explain to them and their parents or carers, as appropriate, why treatment is needed and why any prescribed course should be completed; also advise on prevention and long-term management.
Ensure children and young people and their parents or carers, as appropriate, understand that UTI can recur and that they should remain alert and seek prompt treatment if reinfection is suspected.

Offer children and young people and their parents or carers, as appropriate, information and advice on early symptom recognition; urine collection, storage and testing; treatment choices; prevention; the purpose and nature of urinary tract investigations; prognosis; and the reasons and arrangements for any necessary long-term management.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses diagnosis and management of first or recurrent upper or lower urinary tract infection (UTI) in babies, children and young people under 16. Its aim is more consistent practice through accurate diagnosis and effective management. It does not address people with an indwelling urinary catheter, neurogenic bladder, significant pre-existing urinary tract disorders, underlying renal disease or immunosuppression; recurrent UTI in sexually active girls and young women under 16; or care in intensive care units. Its intended users include healthcare professionals and commissioners, as well as children from birth up to 16 years and their families and carers.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms and signs
document_sections.content: 1.1.1: Test urine when a baby, child or young person has features that raise the likelihood of UTI, using table 1 and its accompanying guidance. [2022] 1.1.2: Consider urine testing when the person is unwell and UTI is suspected even without any feature listed in table 1. [2022] 1.1.3: Refer babies under 3 months with suspected UTI for paediatric specialist care, send urine urgently for microscopy and culture, and follow the specified management sections of the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management. [2017, amended 2022] 1.1.4: Do not routinely test urine in those aged 3 months and over whose features indicate another infection; consider testing if illness persists and the diagnosis remains uncertain. [2022] The features in table 1 guide, rather than determine, whether urine collection and testing are needed: the list is incomplete, an isolated feature in either column need not settle the decision, several features probably increase the likelihood of UTI, and features that lower its likelihood may warrant consideration of another diagnosis. 1.1.5: For a child under 5 with unexplained fever when UTI is no longer suspected, consult the specified NICE fever guideline. [2022] 1.1.6: Paediatric specialists should use that guideline's specialist-management section for decisions about urine testing in children under 5 with fever in their care. [2022] 1.1.7: Collect and test urine without delay; if collection cannot occur at the consultation, advise parents or carers to return a sample as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours. [2022] 1.1.8: Assess and manage suspected sepsis according to the specified NICE sepsis guideline. [2022] 1.1.9: For suspected or confirmed bacterial infection in a baby up to and including 28 days corrected gestational age, follow the specified NICE neonatal-infection guidance, including its relevant early- or late-onset infection sections. [2022] The NICE guideline on child maltreatment provides guidance on considering sexual abuse.

document_sections.heading: Table 1 Symptoms and signs that increase or decrease the likelihood that a UTI is present
document_sections.content: The table separates features associated with a higher likelihood of UTI from features associated with a lower likelihood; it includes symptoms reported by the child or carers as well as clinical findings. It is a decision aid for urine testing, not an exhaustive diagnostic rule.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of risk of serious illness
document_sections.content: 1.1.10: Assess illness severity in babies and children using the clinical-assessment section of the NICE guideline on fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Urine collection
document_sections.content: 1.1.11: Obtain urine from children and young people before administering antibiotics, consistent with the specified NICE antimicrobial-prescribing guidance for acute pyelonephritis and lower UTI. [2022] 1.1.12: Obtain a urine sample in babies and children at high risk of serious illness, but do not postpone treatment when a sample is unobtainable. [2007] 1.1.13: Prefer clean-catch collection wherever feasible. [2007] 1.1.14: If clean catch cannot be achieved, use another non-invasive approach, such as a urine collection pad, according to its manufacturer's directions. [2007] 1.1.15: Do not collect urine from babies or children with cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels. [2007] 1.1.16: If non-invasive collection is impractical or impossible, use catheter sampling or suprapubic aspiration (SPA); before SPA, verify urine is present in the bladder with ultrasound guidance. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Urine preservation
document_sections.content: 1.1.17: Refrigerate immediately or preserve with boric acid a urine specimen intended for culture if culture cannot occur within 4 hours after collection. [2007] 1.1.18: When using boric acid, follow the manufacturer's directions for specimen volume so that the preservative does not potentially suppress bacteria in the sample. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Urine testing
document_sections.content: 1.1.19: In babies and children between 3 months and 3 years with suspected UTI, use a dipstick. If both leukocyte esterase and nitrite are negative, withhold antibiotics and do not request microscopy and culture unless at least 1 criterion in 1.1.21 applies. If either or both are positive, send urine for culture and give antibiotics. [2017] 1.1.20: For children aged 3 years or older, follow table 2 and assess serious-illness risk using the specified NICE fever guideline; age and illness risk affect test selection and interpretation. [2007] Table 2 states that dipstick testing for leukocyte esterase and nitrite is diagnostically comparable to microscopy and culture and can be used safely. 1.1.21: Send urine for culture when acute upper UTI is suspected; serious-illness risk is high to intermediate; the baby is under 3 months; leukocyte esterase or nitrite is positive; UTI recurs; infection has not responded within 24 to 48 hours and no specimen has yet been sent; or clinical findings disagree with the dipstick. [2017] 1.1.22: Interpret microscopy according to table 3. [2007] 1.1.23: When a urine-test result conflicts with clinical findings, use clinical criteria for decisions because a small number of tests may be falsely negative. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Table 2 Urine dipstick testing strategies for children 3 years or older
document_sections.content: The table sets out management for all combinations of positive and negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite results. Depending on the combination and clinical circumstances, it specifies whether to presume or reconsider UTI, prescribe antibiotics, request microscopy or culture, and investigate another cause of illness.

document_sections.heading: Table 3 Interpreting microscopy results
document_sections.content: The table explains how the four positive or negative combinations of pyuria and bacteriuria affect presumptive UTI diagnosis and when symptoms or signs justify starting antibiotics.

document_sections.heading: History and examination of confirmed UTI
document_sections.content: 1.1.24: Document factors associated with UTI or serious underlying disease: poor urine flow; a history suggesting or confirming an earlier UTI; repeated fever without an established cause; a renal abnormality diagnosed antenatally; family history of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) or kidney disease; constipation; dysfunctional voiding; bladder enlargement; an abdominal mass; evidence of a spinal lesion; poor growth; and high blood pressure. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Clinical differentiation between acute upper UTI and lower UTI
document_sections.content: 1.1.25: Presume acute upper UTI in a baby or child with bacteriuria and either a temperature of 38°C or higher, or a temperature lower than 38°C together with loin pain or tenderness. [2007] 1.1.26: Presume lower UTI (cystitis) when bacteriuria occurs without systemic symptoms or signs. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Laboratory tests for localising UTI
document_sections.content: 1.1.27: Do not rely on C-reactive protein by itself to distinguish acute upper from lower UTI in babies and children. [2007]

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Acute management
document_sections.content: Antibiotic requirements for conditions outside this guideline's scope, including known significant pre-existing uropathies, have not been addressed and may differ. 1.2.1: Refer babies and children at high risk of serious illness to a paediatric specialist immediately. [2007] 1.2.2: Immediately refer a baby under 3 months with suspected UTI to a paediatric specialist. [2007] 1.2.3: Paediatric specialists should give parenteral antibiotics to babies under 3 months with suspected UTI in accordance with the specified section of the NICE fever guideline. [2007, amended 2022] 1.2.4: Consider specialist referral for babies and children over 3 months with upper UTI. [2007] 1.2.5: Treat acute upper UTI in those over 3 months with antibiotics according to the NICE guideline on pyelonephritis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing. [2007, amended 2018] 1.2.6: Treat lower UTI in those over 3 months with antibiotics according to the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing. [2007, amended 2018] 1.2.7: For a UTI developing during antibiotic prophylaxis, consult the specified NICE antimicrobial-prescribing guidelines for acute pyelonephritis, lower UTI and recurrent UTI. [2018] 1.2.8: Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in babies and children with antibiotics. [2007] 1.2.9: Laboratories should track urinary-pathogen resistance patterns and routinely provide those findings to prescribers. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Preventing recurrence
document_sections.content: 1.2.10: Address dysfunctional elimination syndromes and constipation in babies and children after UTI. [2007] 1.2.11: Encourage children with a prior UTI to drink sufficient water to prevent dehydration. [2007] 1.2.12: Ensure they can use clean toilets when necessary without avoidable postponement of urination. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Prophylactic antibiotics
document_sections.content: 1.2.13: Do not routinely prescribe antibiotic prophylaxis after a first UTI in babies or children. [2007] 1.2.14: For prophylaxis in recurrent UTI, consult the NICE guideline on urinary tract infection (recurrent): antimicrobial prescribing. [2018] 1.2.15: Do not prescribe antibiotic prophylaxis for asymptomatic bacteriuria in babies or children. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Imaging tests for localising UTI
document_sections.content: 1.2.16: Do not routinely perform imaging solely to determine the location of UTI. [2007] 1.2.17: In the rare situation where confirming or excluding acute upper UTI matters clinically, use power doppler ultrasound; if it is unavailable or leaves the diagnosis unconfirmed, use a dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scintigraphy scan. [2007]

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Imaging tests
document_sections.content: 1.3.1: For atypical UTI, perform urinary tract ultrasound during the acute episode to detect structural problems, including obstruction, and enable prompt management under tables 4, 5 and 6. [2007] 1.3.2: After a first UTI that responds to treatment in a baby younger than 6 months, arrange ultrasound within 6 weeks, according to table 4. [2007] 1.3.3: Do not routinely arrange ultrasound after a treatment-responsive first UTI in babies and children over 6 months unless the episode is atypical, as detailed in tables 5 and 6. [2007] 1.3.4: After lower UTI, arrange ultrasound within 6 weeks only for those younger than 6 months or those with recurrent infections. [2007] 1.3.5: Use a DMSA scan 4 to 6 months after acute infection to identify renal parenchymal defects when indicated by tables 4, 5 and 6. [2007] 1.3.6: If another UTI occurs while awaiting DMSA, reassess the scan date and consider an earlier scan. [2007] 1.3.7: Do not routinely image after UTI to identify VUR, apart from the circumstances in tables 4, 5 and 6. [2007] 1.3.8: If a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) is performed, give oral antibiotic prophylaxis for 3 days and perform MCUG on the second day. [2007] 1.3.9: Apply the imaging schedules in tables 4, 5 and 6 after UTI. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Box 1 Definitions of atypical and recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI)
document_sections.content: Atypical UTI includes serious illness, poor urinary flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, elevated creatinine, septicaemia, failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or infection caused by non-E. coli organisms. Recurrent UTI means Two or more episodes involving acute upper UTI (acute pyelonephritis); One episode of acute upper UTI plus 1 or more episodes of lower UTI (cystitis); or Three or more episodes of lower UTI.

document_sections.heading: Table 4 Recommended imaging schedule for babies younger than 6 months
document_sections.content: The table gives the ultrasound, dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy and micturating cystourethrogram schedule for babies younger than 6 months, separated by response within 48 hours, atypical UTI and recurrent UTI. When a baby with a non-E. coli UTI responds well to antibiotics and has no other atypical feature, a non-urgent ultrasound may instead be requested within 6 weeks.

document_sections.heading: Table 5 Recommended imaging schedule for babies and children between 6 months to under 3 years
document_sections.content: The table distinguishes imaging for treatment response within 48 hours, atypical UTI and recurrent UTI in babies and children from 6 months to under 3 years. Although MCUG is not routine, consider it for ultrasound-detected dilatation, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection or family history of VUR. A non-urgent ultrasound within 6 weeks may be requested for a treatment-responsive non-E. coli UTI without another atypical feature.

document_sections.heading: Table 6 Recommended imaging schedule for children 3 years or older
document_sections.content: The table distinguishes ultrasound, dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy and micturating cystourethrogram schedules for children 3 years or older by treatment response within 48 hours, atypical UTI and recurrent UTI. In toilet-trained children, perform ultrasound with a full bladder and estimate bladder volume before and after urination. A non-urgent ultrasound within 6 weeks may be requested when non-E. coli UTI responds well to antibiotics and no other atypical feature is present.

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Surgical intervention
document_sections.content: 1.4.1: Do not routinely use surgery to manage VUR. [2007]

document_sections.heading: 1.5 Follow up
document_sections.content: 1.5.1: Do not routinely follow up babies and children who have not undergone imaging. [2007] 1.5.2: Agree with parents, carers or the young person, as appropriate, how imaging findings will be communicated. [2007] 1.5.3: Do not routinely offer outpatient follow-up when investigation results are normal. [2007] 1.5.4: Supply parents or carers with written results of every investigation. [2007] 1.5.5: Refer recurrent UTI or abnormal imaging for paediatric specialist assessment. [2007] 1.5.6: In babies and children with renal parenchymal defects, assess height, weight and blood pressure, and routinely test for proteinuria. [2007] 1.5.7: Do not provide long-term follow-up for minor unilateral renal parenchymal defects unless recurrent UTI, family history or lifestyle risk factors for hypertension are present. [2007] 1.5.8: A paediatric nephrologist should monitor and manage bilateral renal abnormalities, impaired kidney function, elevated blood pressure or proteinuria to slow chronic kidney disease progression. [2007] 1.5.9: Do not routinely repeat urine tests for infection after UTI when the baby or child has no symptoms. [2007] 1.5.10: Do not base follow-up solely on asymptomatic bacteriuria. [2007]

document_sections.heading: 1.6 Information and advice
document_sections.content: 1.6.1: When UTI is suspected, healthcare professionals should explain to the child or young person and, as appropriate, their parents or carers why treatment is needed, why any treatment course should be completed, and how to prevent recurrence and manage the condition over time. [2007] 1.6.2: Ensure they understand that UTI can return and that suspected reinfection warrants vigilance and prompt treatment. [2007] 1.6.3: Provide advice about recognising symptoms promptly; collecting, storing and testing urine; treatment choices; prevention; the purpose and nature of urinary tract investigations; prognosis; and the reasons and arrangements for long-term management when needed. [2007]

document_sections.heading: Bacteriuria
document_sections.content: Bacteriuria means bacteria are present in urine, whether or not UTI is present.

document_sections.heading: Fever
document_sections.content: Unless a recommendation specifies otherwise, fever means body temperature above its usual daily variation.

document_sections.heading: Pyuria
document_sections.content: Pyuria means white cells are present in urine.

document_sections.heading: 1 Symptoms and signs of urinary tract infection in children and young people aged 5 years and above but under 16 years
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research to determine which symptoms and signs indicate UTI in children and young people aged 5 years and above but under 16 years. [2022]

document_sections.heading: 2 Long-term risk of renal scarring and impaired renal function
document_sections.content: The committee proposes a well-designed UK cohort study of long-term outcomes, including renal scarring and renal function, in children who have had UTI. [2017]

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: In young children, UTI and VUR have been associated with congenital and acquired renal damage. Progressive scarring is documented in children with high-grade VUR and recurrent UTI. Scarring has been associated with severe hypertension, proteinuria, pregnancy complications and progression to established renal failure. These risks are probably greater with bilateral renal parenchymal defects, but their frequency and magnitude in children with unilateral or bilateral damage remain uncertain. Better estimates of serious or progressive complications would inform management after first-time and recurrent UTI.

document_sections.heading: 3 Symptoms and signs of recurrent UTI
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research on whether UTI symptoms and signs differ between babies, children and young people under 16 years with and without a history of recurrent UTI. [2022]

document_sections.heading: 4 Symptoms and signs of long-term (chronic) UTI
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research into symptoms and signs reported by children and young people with long-term (chronic) UTI and their perceived effects on health and quality of life. [2022]

document_sections.heading: Symptoms and signs
document_sections.content: In its rationale for recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.9, the committee says timely, accurate UTI diagnosis matters for preventing avoidable illness and serious complications such as renal scarring. Table 1 provides greater clarity about features that raise or lower UTI likelihood, including dysuria, urinary frequency, loin tenderness and bedwetting retained from the 2007 guideline. Evidence for many features was low- or very-low quality because studies often were not designed to assess diagnostic accuracy and defined features poorly; the table therefore supplements clinical judgement. Its incomplete list must not prevent testing an unwell person when UTI remains suspected. Studies of algorithms combining features found none particularly accurate, so the committee did not recommend them; multiple features nevertheless probably increase UTI likelihood. Most evidence concerned children under 5 years, and trials seldom separated outcomes by age. The committee considered the features broadly applicable across ages but emphasised that age and communication ability affect their assessment. Dysuria, for example, raised UTI likelihood when present and lowered it when absent across ages, yet can be difficult to assess in a person who cannot communicate or is not toilet trained. Confirmed previous UTI was included despite not itself being a symptom or sign because it raises likelihood. Evidence reviewed did not establish sleepiness or lethargy, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive or jaundice as clinically useful indicators of UTI. Haematuria, cloudy urine and dark urine may be reported by the child or carers before a clinician has a sample; dark urine is not specific and may accompany illness and dehydration, while reported visible blood is, in the committee's view, uncommon in UTI and always needs further investigation. Less specific features may still help when combined. Features that lower UTI likelihood can indicate another infection site but do not rule UTI out. Routine urine testing is unnecessary when another infection is suggested in those aged 3 months and over, although persistent illness with diagnostic uncertainty can warrant testing. The specified fever guideline may assist when an under-5 has otherwise unexplained fever but UTI is no longer suspected. Urine collection and testing should not be delayed; culture can miss some UTIs, for which recommendation 1.1.23 addresses clinical decision-making. Concern about sepsis supports specialist referral and urgent microscopy and culture for suspected UTI under 3 months. Evidence gaps prompted the research questions about ages 5 years and above but under 16 years, recurrent UTI and long-term (chronic) UTI.

document_sections.heading: How the recommendations might affect practice
document_sections.content: The committee expects little substantial change from the 2022 symptom-and-sign recommendations: the diagnostic pathway remains, although some indicative features differ, and no combined-feature algorithm is recommended. It expects little effect on resources or training. It considered the 2017 recommendation likely to clarify practice and make diagnosis more efficient for babies under 3 months.

document_sections.heading: Urine testing
document_sections.content: In its rationale for recommendations 1.1.19 and 1.1.21, the committee reports that, in children aged 3 months or older but younger than 3 years, a dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase or nitrite greatly increases the likelihood of a positive culture. Culturing only positive specimens provided a better balance of benefits and costs than giving antibiotics and obtaining cultures for every child in this age group. Symptoms are easier to recognise at these ages; the committee states that antibiotics should begin only when at least one of those dipstick markers is positive, and positive specimens should also be cultured.

document_sections.heading: How the recommendations might affect practice
document_sections.content: The committee expects dipstick testing at ages 3 months or older but younger than 3 years to clarify its role and support immediate diagnosis and treatment in primary care. It anticipates clearer guidance, more efficient diagnosis, cost savings and fewer specimens sent to laboratories for culture.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: Over the past 30 to 50 years, antibiotics and improvements in healthcare have changed the natural history of childhood UTI, creating uncertainty about optimal management and the justification for investigations and follow-up. UTI is a common bacterial cause of illness in babies and children. Presentation is often nonspecific, especially below 3 years, when urine collection and interpretation are also difficult and definitive confirmation may not always be possible. Imaging, prophylaxis and prolonged follow-up have imposed a substantial burden on NHS resources; the document describes that approach as costly, unpleasant for children, distressing for families and based on limited evidence. The guideline addresses aspects of care from birth up to 16 years.

document_sections.heading: Update information
document_sections.content: July 2022: Following an evidence review, the guideline added diagnostic recommendations for suspected UTI under 16 and a recommendation to collect urine before antibiotics in children and young people; it also clarified and restructured some earlier recommendations. October 2018: Recommendations 1.2.5 and 1.2.6 were aligned with the NICE antimicrobial-prescribing guidance for acute pyelonephritis and lower UTI. September 2017: Evidence on urine-testing strategies under 3 years was reviewed and the urine-testing recommendations were updated.
